title: J.P. Morgan Private Bank expanding in Dallas to tap alternative assets sector - TradingView
content: J.P. Morgan Private Bank, part of banking giant JPMorgan Chase JPM, is expanding its Fund Banking Group with a new hub in Dallas to serve the state's fast-growing private equity, venture capital, and hedge fund communities, the company said Wednesday. "Texas has become a genuine center of gravity for private equity, venture capital, and hedge funds," said Jeff Kaveney, head of Fund Banking at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. "The pace of growth for the region is remarkable, and this new Fund Banking hub responds directly to that momentum." JPMorgan Chase JPM has scaled the private bank platform quickly since it acquired First Republic Bank in 2023. The Private Bank has been serving the private and venture fund spaces and their CEO for 30 years, Kaveney added. The platform has roughly doubled in the past three years. The team now has 40 fund bankers with plans to expand by at least 20% in the next three years. JP Morgan Chase and South Korea’s Hyundai Card are testing AI agents that can negotiate financial transactions and make payments without direct human involvement. While the project could change how corporate payments work, JP Morgan’s early findings suggest that controlling autonomous systems may be harder than building them. According to a CNBC report, the two companies completed an initial proof of concept involving a simulated foreign exchange transaction in which a Hyundai Card AI agent requested a currency exchange to maintain euro liquidity in its deposit account on JP Morgan’s blockchain-based banking platform, Kinexys. The collaboration targets machine-to-machine payments, where AI systems, without a person in the loop, recommend actions, initiate and approve transfers, and verify their authenticity. A second phase, planned for the first half of 2027, will look at how multiple AI agents can interact, negotiate agreements, and settle payments with one another. Wee Kee Toh, global head of Kinexys Insights, told CNBC that the goal is to see what happens when agents move beyond just carrying out tasks and start dealing with each other. The technical challenge includes ensuring that these payment agents can sift through complex regulatory frameworks to stay within the laws of different jurisdictions, as well as detect fraud in real time. They must also handle edge cases that could confuse algorithms while maintaining clear audit trails to meet compliance requirements. However, the executive pointed out that developing the technology was the easy part, while establishing governance and internal controls could prove more difficult. According to a recent report by AvePoint, at least 34% of security breaches linked to AI agents were due to unauthorized autonomous actions, including them making transactions and data changes without human approval. Furthermore, AvePoint CEO Tianyi Jiang warned that interactions between AI agents could allow a compromised or malfunctioning agent to pass incorrect information to others and possibly trigger a chain of unauthorized actions. Recall that in October, OpenAI revealed that a research model took funds without permission from a developer’s wallet on the Ethereum testnet to pay for deployment fees. Regarding the concerns mentioned above, Toh pointed out that companies using the system can put guardrails around agents so that, for example, if an agent is authorized to transact up to $5 million, any requests above that amount will be rejected automatically. “You are going to draw a box around the agent. The agent will never be able to do anything out of the box,” he said. Alongside spending limits, Hassan Ahmed, Coinbase’s Singapore country director, added that safe agent payment should also have restricted account permissions and clear authorization requirements, and give users the ability to monitor activity and revoke access at any time. Barnum will become vice chairman and remain with the company until early 2028. The latest leadership reshuffle comes as JPMorgan continues preparing its management team for the eventual retirement of longtime CEO Jamie Dimon, raising questions about whether the bank's succession strategy is gradually taking shape. De Best, who joined JPMorgan in 2006, has extensive experience across banking, markets and finance and should support financial oversight, capital allocation and strategic decision-making across the bank’s diversified operations. The CFO transition follows several senior management changes aimed at strengthening JPMorgan's leadership pipeline. In January 2025, Jennifer Piepszak was named chief operating officer, succeeding Daniel Pinto, who announced plans to retire by the end of 2026. Further, in June 2026, JPMorgan appointed Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh as co-presidents. Petno assumed sole leadership of CIB, while Rohrbaugh became CEO of Consumer & Community Banking following Marianne Lake's decision to retire. These moves suggest JPMorgan is positioning experienced executives in critical leadership roles while ensuring management continuity. The staggered transitions also provide executives with opportunities to demonstrate their capabilities across major business divisions. A stable leadership bench could help sustain investor confidence as Jamie Dimon remains CEO for now. Dimon, the longest-tenured CEO among major U.S. banks, has led the bank for more than two decades and has no immediate plans to step down. Nonetheless, the latest CFO appointment, alongside earlier leadership changes, signals a deliberate effort to build a robust succession framework. Two close peers of JPM are Bank of America BAC and Citigroup C. Bank of America has strengthened its succession planning by appointing Dean Athanasia and Jim DeMare as co-presidents in September 2025, while elevating CFO Alastair Borthwick to executive vice president. title: JPMorgan is working on AI agent transactions that don’t involve humans - CNBC
content:
Artificial intelligence agents have already proven to be helpful, or cause a lot of trouble, or both. One area seen as high-potential is in payments, where — if they’re able to be trusted — the agents could deal with all sorts of money matters on behalf of people. That’s why JPMorgan Chase and South Korea’s Hyundai Card are testing how AI agents can handle financial transactions without direct human intervention, including whether they can eventually negotiate and make payments with one another. The companies have completed an initial proof-of-concept involving a simulated foreign exchange transaction and are targeting the first half of 2027 for a more complex phase involving multiple AI agents. Wee Kee Toh, global head of Kinexys Insights at Kinexys by JP Morgan, told CNBC that the next step is to test what happens when autonomous agents move beyond execution and begin interacting with each other in an ecosystem. “That, I would say, is really the biggest part of what we want to get as an expansion of the phase one scope,” he added. The initial trial involved a Hyundai Card AI agent requesting a foreign exchange transaction to maintain euro liquidity in its Kinexys blockchain deposit account. JPMorgan said it was the first private blockchain-based autonomous bank-agent-to-client-agent test for corporate treasury management. While the initial trial has been completed, JPMorgan has yet to set a timeline for commercializing the technology. Toh said building the technology itself was relatively straightforward, but establishing appropriate governance and internal controls proved more difficult. “Technology-wise, it’s really not the biggest hurdle,” he said, pointing instead to questions around accountability and the risks of allowing AI agents to execute financial transactions without direct human oversight. However, the potential of such agents to change interactions with financial services has to come with equivalent accountability, according to experts. Data management and protection software company AvePoint found in its State of AI 2026 report that unauthorized autonomous agent actions were the third most common AI agent-related security breach, affecting 34.1% of companies that reported such incidents. Those actions included executing transaction and modifying data without approval, though the findings were not isolated to corporate treasury payments. “When agents negotiate and execute autonomously … governance shifts from monitoring human behavior to monitoring machine-to-machine dependencies,” said AvePoint CEO Tianyi Jiang. Jiang explained that interacting AI agents could amplify errors and trigger transactions before humans can intervene. “The worst-case scenario is a cascading failure where one compromised or hallucinating agent feeds bad data to another,” he said, potentially “triggering a high-speed chain reaction of flawed financial transfers before a human even realizes it is happening.” To address such concerns, Kinexys developed a framework that restricts AI agents to predefined transaction parameters, automatically rejecting requests that fall outside authorized limits. “You are going to draw a box around the agent. The agent will never be able to do anything out of the box,” Toh said. For example, an AI agent authorized to transact up to $5 million would be blocked from executing transactions above that threshold, he said. Hassan Ahmed, Coinbase’s Singapore country director, said safe agentic payments will require clear guardrails, including spending limits, restricted account permissions and explicit authorization requirements. Users should also be able to monitor activity and revoke access at any time, he said, given the potential for AI to create new opportunities for malicious actors. “While private or permissioned environments may offer additional controls for certain use cases, we should not lose sight of the potential of open blockchain networks to support more accessible, interoperable and efficient financial systems,” Ahmed said. JPMorgan and Hyundai Card are also exploring whether to extend their collaboration to other businesses within Hyundai Motor Group, whose broader operations were one reason the bank selected the credit card company as a partner, Toh said. No specific projects have been announced. Hyundai Motor Group holds a combined 78.04% stake in Hyundai Card through Hyundai Motor, Kia and Hyundai Commercial, according to the card issuer’s website. Hyundai Card has previously experimented with blockchain-based cross-border payments. In July, the company said it completed a proof-of-concept involving a $20,000 transfer using the USDT stablecoin between Hyundai Motor’s U.S. and Mexican subsidiaries, with the transfer and verification process taking an average of seven minutes. Kinexys has also been expanding its blockchain-based payments business. The JPMorgan unit said in August that it had processed more than $4 trillion in transactions since inception, averaging about $7 billion a day. Separately, JPMorgan launched a proof-of-concept for its dollar-denominated deposit token, JPMD, in June 2025, before making it available to institutional clients that November. JPMorgan Chase (JPM) said Tuesday that longtime CFO Jeremy Barnum will step down next year in the latest change among the top ranks of the country's largest bank as it prepares for CEO Jamie Dimon's eventual succession. Barnum, who has served as the bank's CFO since 2021, will be succeeded by Bregje de Best, CFO of JPMorgan's commercial and investment bank, after the company's first quarter earnings in April, according to a JPMorgan filing. Barnum will become vice chair, remaining with the bank until early 2028, JPMorgan said. Dimon added in a press release statement that Barnum had requested the transition after six years in the role. That tenure is slightly above average for a CFO at a large US company, according to a 2025 study by executive search firm Spencer Stuart, which found CFOs at S&P 500 companies had served an average of 4.8 years in their positions. The announcement comes less than a week after Allison Beer, JPMorgan's head of credit card and connected commerce, informed colleagues that she was leaving to pursue another opportunity, according to an internal JPMorgan memo. It also follows a broader leadership shake-up of Dimon's top lieutenants earlier this year when JPMorgan announced the retirement of Marianne Lake, the former head of its sprawling consumer bank and previously a leading candidate to succeed Dimon. This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed. The announcement of Lake's departure also came as JPMorgan said it was elevating executives Doug Petno and Troy Rohrbaugh to the role of co-president, signaling their leads to eventually take the reins from Dimon, who was expected to stay for three more years as CEO, according to an executive familiar with the matter who spoke to Yahoo Finance at the time. Barnum's planned transition and Lake's retirement are part of a broader effort to prepare JPMorgan's next generation of leadership, according to a person familiar with the bank's succession planning. The person characterized Beer's departure as separate, saying the credit card executive was seeking a broader leadership role than her current responsibilities at the bank. De Best, 43, joined JPMorgan in 2006 and has held senior positions across investment banking, markets and corporate banking. She will also join the firm's operating committee when she assumes the CFO role. Morgan Stanley analyst Manan Gosalia said Tuesday his team "do[es] not expect the CFO transition itself to have any impact on JPM's strategy or preliminary 2027 outlook." RBC Capital Markets analyst Gerard Cassidy also told clients Tuesday, in reaction to Barnum's departure, that senior management shake-ups are not unusual at JPMorgan. "We expect JPM's deep management bench will continue to enable the company to effectively manage through senior executive realignment," Cassidy said. content: JPMorgan Chase (JPM) announced on Tuesday that Bregje de Best, the current chief financial officer of its Commercial & Investment Bank (CIB), will succeed Jeremy Barnum as the banking giant’s CFO following its first-quarter 2027 financial reporting. Barnum, who has served as CFO since May 2021, informed the bank of his decision to step down after six years and help transition financial leadership. Barnum will oversee the bank’s January and April earnings announcements as well as February Investor Day before becoming Vice Chairman. He will remain in that position until early 2028. Barnum was appointed CFO on May 18, 2021, succeeding Jennifer Piepszak. During his tenure, JPMorgan acquired First Republic Bank for $10.60 billion. “Jeremy has been an outstanding CFO of our company since 2021 and is enormously respected both internally by our leadership team and employees as well as outside the company by investors, analysts and others,” CEO Jamie Dimon said. During his tenure, the bank reported earnings beats in 17 of the 22 quarters, according to Koyfin. JPM shares gained more than 105% since his appointment. De Best has overseen financial management and controls across JPMorgan’s banking, markets, payments and securities services businesses since June last year. Prior to that, she co-led Global Corporate Banking and held senior roles in the UK and Asia. The bank plans to name de Best’s successor early next year. JPMorgan reported an 8% increase in third-quarter (Q3) revenue to $50.2 billion, but it missed Wall Street’s estimate of about $51.22 billion, according to Fiscal.ai. title: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq Futures Mixed Ahead Of Much-Anticipated Nvidia Earnings, Anthropic IPO: SLS, BABA, JPM, OMER In Focus - Stocktwits
content: U.S. stock futures traded mixed overnight late Monday as markets gear up for Nvidia Corp.’s (NVDA) third-quarter earnings on Tuesday and Anthropic's much-anticipated public listing on Wednesday. As of 10:37 p.m. EST, Dow futures declined 0.26%, while the S&P 500 futures gained 0.12% and Nasdaq-100 futures climbed 0.67%. On Monday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes closed lower amid a tech rout. The Nasdaq Composite led the decline, shedding more than 600 points to close 2.49% lower. The S&P 500 lost 1.92% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.41%. On Monday, markets took a beating as investors sold off Nvidia ahead of its Q3 results. The stock plunged more than 4% at close, dragging down other AI stocks and chipmakers. Nvidia’s results will need to prove that demand for its AI chips remains strong and that its growth outlook can sustain despite the recent leadership upheaval. New U.S. restrictions on China’s access to advanced AI chips and offshore computing power added to concerns over Nvidia’s leadership crisis and AI financing risks. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) fell more than 5% at close, while Micron Technology Inc. (MU) tumbled more than 7%. Broadcom Inc. (AVGO), Intel Corp. (INTC) and Marvell Technology Inc. (MRVL) also posted significant losses. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) and iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) also slumped about 5% each on Monday, while the Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF (MAGS) fell 2.51%. Charlie Bilello, Chief Market Strategist at Creative Planning, highlighted the sharp slide in NVDA stock following CEO Jensen Huang’s infidelity reports. In a post on X, he said, “Oct 6, 2026: Nvidia was up 28% YTD with a $5.8 trillion market cap, the world's largest. Today: After a 35% drawdown, Nvidia is now down 16% YTD with a market cap of $3.8 trillion. And Apple has reclaimed the world's top spot. $2 trillion erased in the last six weeks.” Meanwhile, Hideyuki Ishiguro, chief strategist at Nomura Asset Management, told Bloomberg that “Tighter restrictions could raise concerns about slowing sales growth and may weigh on earnings in the short term” for Asian chip-related firms. A potential catalyst for markets this week is Claude-maker Anthropic’s public listing, expected on Wednesday. The AI giant’s valuation could top $1.4 trillion, stoking a key test for Wall Street's AI appetite. Analyst Michaël van de Poppe said in a post on X, “Honestly, I think that the Anthropic IPO is likely going to go up first and then sideways, just like the SpaceX IPO. As a result, liquidity should flow back in due time.” Kenny Polcari, Chief Market Strategist at Slatestone Wealth, said in a post on X that the real test will be “how much future growth is already priced in—and what investors will pay for the AI boom,” even as its IPO is over 6x oversubscribed. On the geopolitical front, U.S. Vice President JD Vance vowed that the conflict with Iran would not become a prolonged “forever war” lasting two years. He also maintained that he remains aligned with Trump on Iran, acknowledged that the war contributed to Republican midterm losses through higher energy prices, and attributed those costs partly to decades of underinvestment in US energy infrastructure. Meanwhile, fresh attacks on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and a drone alert at a major gas field in northern Iraq have been reported late Monday, raising security concerns in the pivotal shipping route and the prolonged tensions between the U.S. and Iran despite diplomatic efforts to end the war. Chip stocks eased in post-market hours on Monday after a sharp drop in the regular session triggered by new U.S. chip curbs targeting AI capacity available to Chinese companies. SK Hynix (SKHY) led the overnight gains, rising 3.6%. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Micron (MU) rose 2% and 2.8% respectively and Broadcom (AVGO) gained 2.3% in what appears to be a relief rally. AMD, MU and AVGO fell between 4% and 7.6% in Monday’s session as investors took the new U.S. technology export curbs as a potential headwind for chip sales. Intel (INTC), which fell 7%, continued to be in the red in overnight trading as Nvidia disclosed it trimmed its stake in the government-backed chipmaker. The Donald Trump administration on Monday moved to limit several countries from providing Chinese companies remote access to advanced AI chips and servers, following increased scrutiny over its handling of curbs on semiconductor exports after an alleged spy scandal involving Nvidia Corp (NVDA). An interim rule issued by the Commerce Department now requires data center operators in Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil to obtain a license from Washington before exporting advanced AI chips from Nvidia and other U.S. manufacturers to customers in those countries. The measure is an attempt to restrict China and other U.S. adversaries from accessing offshore computing power that uses high-end American processors. The government’s directive came days after Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following his admission to an affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed International whom the U.S. authorities suspect of being a Chinese spy. Megaspeed was already under a U.S. investigation for possible export control violations. Nvidia will report third-quarter results on Tuesday and will likely face tough questions about Huang and the chipmaker's dealings with Megaspeed. SemiAnalysis founder Dylan Patel said more than 1.5 gigawatts of chips are in China in violation of U.S. law, and warned that efforts to trace how they got there could reshape the AI industry. “That whole web” is now set to unwind, he said in a SemiAnalysis video interview. Patel also questioned whether open-source AI can thrive if Nvidia can no longer support it, calling the ecosystem “a lot weaker with NVIDIA down and out.” He said that shift could leave Anthropic closer to a monopoly or duopoly, a prospect he said “bodes really well” for its IPO this week, although Anthropic is “more diverse in what chips they use than any other company in the world.” Meanwhile, Nvidia disclosed its latest holdings. It cut its stake in Intel by 25% in the third quarter, selling about 53.69 million shares, and now holds 161.08 million shares. The disclosure weighed on Intel’s shares in post market hours. Nvidia also trimmed positions in Nokia and Synopsys during the quarter, while increasing its SpaceX stake. To be sure, investors such as Soros Fund Management, Barclays and Assenagon Asset Management increased their Intel stakes in Q3. On Stocktwits, the retail sentiment was ‘extremely bullish’ for BABA, ‘bullish’ for AMD and AVGO, ‘neutral’ for MU, and ‘bearish’ for INTC. “$INTC Unfortunately, we have some gullible investors who are selling after every panic-inducing post/article. Bitcoin (BTC) is struggling to find its footing after the weekend selloff, and the options market is showing signals on the downside. With Nvidia (NVDA) set to report earnings after market close on Tuesday, rising Treasury yields and weakening spot Bitcoin ETF flows are adding to concerns for the cryptocurrency’s performance. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 on Friday and plummeted to around $62,000 over the weekend, before recovering to $64,000 late Monday. Now analysts warn that a weak report from Nvidia could push it below $60,000. Nicolai Søndergaard, a research analyst at Nansen, said the $60,000 to $62,600 range is the key test in the next few weeks. Nvidia's disappointing report could spark another wave of selling across risk assets, he said. "AI and crypto draw on the same pool of risk capital, so when Nvidia sells off, the money goes to cash, not into bitcoin," Søndergaard told Coindesk. Søndergaard is looking for a break above the 200-day moving average near $73,000 as the first sign that the selling is done. Bitcoin’s price was trading at $64,490, down over 1% in the last 24 hours. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around BTC dropped to the ‘bearish’ zone from the ‘neutral’ zone over the past day. Chatter around it rose over 38% over the past week, according to platform data. The Over-the-Counter (OTC) desk of crypto market maker Wintermute, which facilitates large trades away from public exchanges, said that Bitcoin is still in a bear market. Coindesk reported that the desk sees little sign of new inflows in to fuel a recovery. The OTC desk said rising rates have changed how investors treat Bitcoin. "This is a rates tape in which bitcoin is the non-yielding funding leg, the ETF bid is gone and the technicals have broken, so we stay defensive and the path of least resistance still feels lower,” the desk added. Wintermute predicts Bitcoin to face pressure around the $50,000 range. The next levels to watch were identified as $62,000 and then $60,000. The desk said much of the pressure is coming from the bond market. Traders see about a 92% chance the Federal Reserve will again raise rates in December. The 10-year Treasury yield is up to 5.15%. This makes holding an asset that pays no interest, like Bitcoin, more difficult. The two calls among the top eight were the $65,000 and $75,000 strikes expiring Dec. 25. The $75,000 call jumped 46.67%, a sign some traders are betting on a bounce. Nvidia agreed to invest $1 billion in Nokia in October 2025, paying $6.01 a share for a 2.9% stake. The investment came with a partnership to run Nokia’s 5G and future 6G network software on Nvidia chips. The companies also agreed to explore using Nokia’s optical technology and switches to move data through Nvidia’s AI infrastructure. The partnership continued after Nvidia reduced its holdings: Last month, Nokia reported progress in using Nvidia chips to process radio signals and bring AI services closer to mobile users, highlighting its work with European operators including BT, Deutsche Telekom, Elisa and Orange. In the same quarter Nvidia cut its stake, Nokia’s sales to AI and cloud customers rose 123% from a year ago, and orders from those customers grew 118%. On Monday, Nokia teamed up with Nscale, Skeleton, Telia and Verda to form AI Gigafactory Northern. The group plans to bid for an EU contract to build and operate a network of computing sites that European businesses, researchers and public agencies could use to run AI workloads. Nokia will supply the networking equipment to move data securely between the sites. The partners have selected Oulu in Finland, Iru in Estonia and Valmiera in Latvia, and are still choosing a location in Sweden. Additionally, Nokia signed a multiyear agreement licensing its video tech for use in ASUS devices. The deal resolves all related patent litigation between the companies. Nokia has contributed to several generations of video compression standards, which help devices store and stream video using less data. The companies kept the financial terms confidential. Shares of Sellas Life Sciences (SLS) jumped up to 12% in extended trading on Monday as traders weighed Lilly’s Calytrix deal against Sellas’s valuation, while filings showed that Susquehanna and Prudential added 1.3 million shares in Q3. SLS stock slid 5% on Monday to $7.47, logging its third straight session of losses. Eli Lilly (LLY) agreed on Monday to pay up to $1.5 billion for Calytrix Bio, whose lead drug has yet to enter human trials. Lilly’s potential maximum payout was close to Sellas’ entire $1.52 billion market value at Monday’s close, and its lead leukemia drug is already awaiting Phase 3 results. Calytrix is developing an antibody that targets a mutation behind two rare blood cancers, essential thrombocythemia and myelofibrosis. Lilly will make an undisclosed upfront payment. How much Calytrix shareholders ultimately receive depends on whether the drug reaches clinical and regulatory milestones. It was Lilly’s second deal this year involving an experimental myelofibrosis treatment. In April, the drugmaker agreed to pay up to $2.3 billion for Ajax Therapeutics, whose lead drug was in Phase 1 testing. Sellas’s lead drug, Galinpepimut-S (GPS), targets a different blood cancer. Its Phase 3 Regal trial is testing whether the immunotherapy helps patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) live longer after their disease goes into remission for a second time. Last month, Sellas said that the trial had reached its 80th death, the threshold set for the final survival analysis. Last week, Sellas said that it expected results in November. “If successful, we believe GPS could be a transformative new immunotherapy for AML patients in second complete remission,” CEO Angelos Stergiou said. A second leukemia drug, Tambiciclib (SLS009), also has results due this quarter. Sellas had enrolled 40 of a planned 80 patients in a Phase 2 trial for newly diagnosed AML. In December, it plans to present findings from a separate study in patients whose leukemia returned or resisted treatment. title: Why Are US Banks Reporting Outages? JPMorgan Rules Out Cyberattack, Blames Software Bug - TradingView
content: Users at multiple American banks, including JPMorgan Chase & Co. (JPM), reported outages of banking services late Monday, with some retail users speculating about a cybersecurity attack. However, JPMorgan denied evidence of cybersecurity attacks and attributed the outage to a software bug. According to DownDetector, apart from JPMorgan, service disruptions were also reported at Bank of America Corp. (BAC), Wells Fargo & Co. (WFC), Capital One Financial Corp. (COF), and U.S. Bancorp. (USB). As per the website, 33% of the issues reported at JPMorgan were related to the website, while 32% reported issues with fund transfers and 20% reported login troubles. Meanwhile, at Wells Fargo, users reported challenges with account balances or transactions, login and digital payment service Zelle. At Bank of America, US Bank and Capital One, troubles ranged from ATM and online banking to app-related issues. JPMorgan said in a post on X, “JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems – there is no evidence this is cyber-related. It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.” The bank added that as a party to transactions involving other banks, those banks may have been impacted as well, but clarified that this was not a systemic issue. “Customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We’re working diligently to resolve this by the end of the day today,” it said. Banking Outage Follows Disruptions At Microsoft, FAA Last Week The issues at JPMorgan and other banks come shortly after Microsoft Corp. (MSFT) suffered a widespread outage across Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services on Thursday, which continued into Friday last week. Meanwhile, a technical network overload caused by a router update and data flood forced the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13, 2026, halting all flight departures across U.S. airports for nearly five hours. Retail users on Stocktwits acknowledged the “weird” coincidence of multiple outages within a short period of time across industries. One user said, “$QQQ $SPY First $MSFT is down, Then FAA gets affected. Now the "bugs" are hitting $JPM. What's next, ATMs down (unable to process withdrawls)?” Another user said, “$JPM AI has become the boogey man ...any glitch etc is bc of ai. Its mass hysteria. But thats what kept us from forming a bubble in the stock market.” A third user said, “$JPM just sayin seems weird this last week.” JPM stock is down about 0.15% overnight, while WFC has lost about 0.17%, and COF and USB are trading marginally higher in the same time. title: JP Morgan Chase Wins North American Corporate Chess League Season 14 - Chess.com
content: JP Morgan Chase won the 14th season of the North American Corporate Chess League in an exciting final match against PWC, taking the title 3-2. It was the banking company's first championship. The company fielded a strong team led by IM Edward Song, FMs Alex Bian and Maggie Feng, NM Asuka Nakamura (brother of GM Hikaru Nakamura), and Calvin Yang. You can see coverage of the knockout matches, hosted by GM Kayden Troff, below. A successful regular season earned JP Morgan Chase the top seed entering the knockout phase. In the quarterfinals they faced the tech company NVIDIA, led by IM Bogdan-Gabriel Vioreanu. Song faced technical issues to start the playoffs and forfeited his game against Vioreanu. That was the only victory for NVIDIA, while Yang and Nakamura scored for JP Morgan Chase to take a tight match, 3-2. In the semifinals, JP Morgan Chase faced Susquehanna, who had defeated the defending champions, Jane Street, in the previous round. Nakamura led the way again with a critical victory, while Bian defeated Brian Luo in a sharp game. Nicolas Brinkman struck back for Susquehanna by defeating Yang, but it wasn't enough. JP Morgan Chase advanced 3-2, earning a spot in the finals. PWC was led by GM Andrey Baryshpolets, and they defeated Meta to earn a finals matchup against JP Morgan Chase. Baryshpolets defeated Song in a complicated game, and PWC's Mark Morrison moved to 3/3 on the day by defeating Yang. JP Morgan Chase struck on the other boards. Nakamura won his third game of the day, defeating NM David Siamon. Bian defeated Michael Giampa and Feng defeated Alexander Fogel in a tricky endgame. Feng's victory clinched the title for JP Morgan Chase, winning the match 3-2 and bringing the company its first title in the 14-year history of the league. The North American Corporate Chess League brings together companies headquartered in the U.S., Canada, and Mexico for seven weeks of team chess competition on Chess.com. title: Lilly secures another myelofibrosis option via $1.5B deal for JPM-founded Calytrix - Fierce Biotech
content: Eli Lilly has added another myelofibrosis (MF) play to its pipeline courtesy of a $1.5 billion deal for Massachusetts biotech Calytrix Bio. The prize for Lilly is a biparatopic antibody for mutant calreticulin (mCALR)-driven essential thrombocythemia (ET) and MF, which are both rare blood cancers. Calytrix has touted the preclinical antibody as a way to deliver “disease-modifying pan-mutant activity, with a safety and convenience profile that supports early intervention and long-term treatment.” While current treatments for ET and MF primarily manage symptoms and complications, Calytrix spied an opportunity for a precision therapy targeting the CALR mutation that drives the disease. Under the deal, Calytrix’s shareholders could receive up to $1.5 billion cash spread across upfront and milestone payments—although the companies didn’t offer a detailed breakdown of the financials. Lilly already has an MF asset in its pipeline courtesy of the phase 1-stage type II JAK2 inhibitor AJ1-11095 which was the focus of the Big Pharma’s $2.3 billion deal for Ajax Therapeutics in April. That bet appeared to pay off two months later when 70% of patients achieved a best response of at least a 35% reduction in spleen volume in early results from a phase 1 study. In a note to investors this morning, Citi analysts suggested that Calytrix’s preclinical asset was a good strategic fit alongside AJ1-11095, as the newly acquired candidate targets the disease-driving clone rather than downstream JAK signaling. “The biparatopic design targets both major mCALR mutation types, which together are found in roughly one-quarter of ET and primary MF patients,” the analysts noted. “While scientifically attractive, the program remains preclinical, and the safety bar will be particularly high in indolent ET.” “An mCALR-specific antibody could be evaluated alone or potentially alongside a JAK2 inhibitor, although combination strategy, dosing and the ability to reverse established marrow fibrosis remain unproven,” the analysts concluded. Calytrix was built last year by J.P. Morgan’s life sciences venture capital arm with a mission to develop disease-modifying therapies for patients living with myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs). “Calytrix was founded on the belief that patients with MPNs deserve therapies that do more than manage symptoms,” the biotech’s CEO Brad Prosek said in a Nov. 16 release. “From the beginning, our goal has been to alter the disease course in mCALR-driven ET and MF,” Prosek added. “We look forward to Lilly advancing the program through the clinic and exploring its potential to benefit patients across the disease spectrum.” The Calytrix acquisition caps off a hectic year of buyouts for Lilly. Fueled by sales of its GLP-1 drugs, the company has inked a series of takeovers and licensing pacts, penning multibillion-dollar deals with biotechs including AtaiBeckley, Centessa Pharmaceuticals and Kelonia Therapeutics.

AI capital now costs more, making selective infrastructure lending and ownership of businesses advancing AI in public and private markets crucial. NEW YORK, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- J.P. Morgan Private Bank today released its 2027 Global Investment Outlook, The Price of Progress, which identifies the convergence of artificial intelligence, global fragmentation and inflation as driving a historic repricing of capital and giving investors greater pricing power. "For much of the last cycle, investors could overlook the cost of capital. The next phase of progress demands a closer look," said Grace Peters, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. "Today, technology companies, governments and consumers are all competing for the same limited pool of capital, and investors are setting the price. Every financing must now clear a higher bar." "That pricing power gives investors a position of strength, but it also makes allocation decisions more consequential," added Stephen Parker, Co-Head of Global Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank. "With cash earning a real return, every investment must justify the capital committed to it. The question is not simply where opportunity exists, but where investors are being paid enough to pursue it." The 2027 Global Investment Outlook explores how investors must decide who to lend to, what to own and at what price across artificial intelligence, global fragmentation and inflation. For much of the post-financial crisis cycle, zero rates and quantitative easing kept financing costs low. That backdrop has changed. Inflation remained above central bank targets through 2026, bond yields climbed to multi-decade highs, and a global rate-hiking cycle took hold, with 17 of 37 central banks we track now in a hiking posture. Yet yields were rising ahead of policy moves, underscoring the role investors now play in setting the price of capital. "Central banks will remain pivotal in 2027. How far they raise rates matters — but policy rates are only part of the story," said Parker. "With investment grade yields above 6% for the first time since the financial crisis, today's starting point for high grade credit is more compelling than it has been in years, even if rates rise further." "Higher yields strengthen the case for a traditional stock-bond portfolio, but a balanced portfolio is only the beginning," continued Parker. "Forward-looking returns for stocks and bonds are the most attractive they have been in years, but AI uncertainty, inflation risk and historic equity concentration all argue for going further. Real assets, hedge funds and private markets have moved from a complement to a necessity." Global Fragmentation Raises the Demand for Capital Security, resilience and regional alignment are increasingly taking precedence over efficiency. Governments, many already carrying substantial debt and deficits, need capital to strengthen security, build AI ecosystems, and secure energy supplies. As those demands grow, investors have more consequential choices to make about where, and on what terms, to provide it. "Resilience is a durable investment theme, but it will not reward capital equally in every market," said Peters. "Assessing sovereigns' defense and AI capabilities, exposure to supply-chain chokepoints and climate vulnerability can help identify where capital may be best positioned for the era of global fragmentation. Since every bloc has vulnerabilities, concentration in any one is probably not prudent." "In the United States, fiscal capacity and natural resources continue to underpin confidence for Treasuries and the dollar, while Europe's stronger corporate earnings make equities more compelling than sovereign debt," continued Peters. "Across Asia, Korea and Taiwan play critical roles in chip manufacturing, while Latin America offers opportunities ranging from nearshoring in Mexico to commodity exposure elsewhere." The AI buildout remains constrained by scarcity rather than excess capacity, but the debate is shifting from infrastructure capacity to monetization and political risk. By the early 2030s, the global data center fleet will need to generate roughly $3.0 trillion a year in end-customer revenue to break even, a high bar, but one we believe the AI ecosystem can clear. Meanwhile, AI-related debt issuance is expected to top $300 billion this year, still largely investment grade, but newer, less transparent structures are making AI more expensive to fund. "The boom will only continue if investors bridge the gap between infrastructure spending and durable revenue," said Parker. "Not every layer of the AI stack carries the same risk or deserves the same capital. That means being deliberate about where in the AI ecosystem your capital goes, not just whether you participate in it." We believe that hyperscalers are the best-positioned public equity exposure, given their ability to benefit whether compute is scarce or abundant. The infrastructure and semiconductor layers warrant more caution, especially given more political hurdles to data center construction. Investment grade AI-related debt offers the most risk-managed entry point, while the application layer, frontier labs and AI-native software, holds the most compelling long-term upside, best accessed selectively through private markets. title: DBS, JP Morgan interlink tokenized deposits for 24/7 USD payments - Ledger Insights
content: DBS and JP Morgan have launched connectivity between their separate tokenized deposit solutions, supporting institutional and corporate clients making 24/7 payments in USD across banks and between the US and Singapore. One of the challenges of single bank tokenized deposits is that they only work among clients of the same bank. This solution is available to clients that use JP Morgan’s Kinexys Digital Payments and DBS Token Services, with Ant International as the inaugural customer. Ant has helped launch several tokenized deposit solutions, as well as tokenized money market funds of late. Last year the two banks announced plans for a standard to enable interoperability between tokenized deposits. The two banks already have a close relationship as co-founders of the DLT payments network Partior, alongside Temasek. For this interconnectivity, Partior is handling settlement orchestration. With several other banks now involved in Partior, including Standard Chartered and Deutsche Bank, the model could in theory be replicated. Something similar could also be achieved with DBS simply using a nostro account on JP Morgan’s Kinexys Digital Payments. With Partior the transactions are synchronized, Partior provides a more neutral venue, and the solution is repeatable across different banks and currencies. But that does raise the question of why this interconnectivity was only launched with USD and not SGD. Want the full story? title: Inflation, a fragmented world and the next phase of AI: Where investors may find risk and opportunity in 2027 - Chase Bank

As 2026 draws to a close, investors have had to navigate an unusual mix of market gains and mounting pressures. The S&P 500 has reached new record highs, even as conflict in the Middle East disrupted energy markets, inflation remained above central bank targets and bond yields climbed. Meanwhile, enthusiasm for AI has continued to drive investment – along with tougher questions about what returns that spending will ultimately generate. Inflation, global fragmentation and AI are not new themes, having previously anchored our 2026 Mid-Year Outlook. But heading into 2027, the growing need to finance AI and security is changing what it costs to invest in them – and what investors can earn in return. Technology companies need capital to build AI infrastructure, while governments need it to strengthen defense, energy security and supply chains. At the same time, inflation and higher interest rates have made financing more expensive but have also given investors more choices about where to put their money. What they choose to fund – and at what price – will help shape the next phase of progress. In its newly released 2027 Outlook, J.P. Morgan Wealth Management examines how these forces may shape markets and investment decisions in the year ahead. “The three forces of AI, fragmentation, and inflation have been validated throughout 2026 through the dramatic AI capex and earnings super cycle, the energy supply shock of the U.S. / Iran conflict, and through central banks that have been forced to tighten policy to promote inflation-fighting credibility,” J.P. Morgan Wealth Management’s Chief Investment Strategist Phil Camporeale said. “Simply put, these three forces appear to be deepening rather than fading. Through all of this, we remain constructive on diversified multi-asset portfolios heading into 2027, but that constructive view depends on a few key assumptions.” The opportunities are significant, but they are not all alike. Here’s what investors should watch for in 2027. Inflation may moderate in 2027, but that does not mean a return to the low interest rate environment that investors grew accustomed to before the pandemic. Energy prices have added to inflation pressures, and central banks are weighing how far they might need to raise rates. Slower wage growth and a stable labor market suggest policymakers may be able to contain inflation without bringing the economic expansion to an end. For investors, higher rates cut both ways. They make it more expensive for companies and governments to borrow, but they also change what investors can earn when they lend. The challenge is to take advantage of that shift while remaining prepared for another potential inflation shock. "We assume that central bankers are hiking rates as part of a mid-cycle adjustment to maintain credibility," said Camporeale. "We don’t anticipate the kind of aggressive hiking that often accompanies the end of a business cycle." Central banks may not need to raise rates aggressively. Slower wage growth and a stable labor market support the view that inflation could moderate without a sharp rate-hiking campaign. Faster wage growth could change that calculation, however. A sustained energy shock poses a different problem: It could push prices higher while weakening demand, leaving central banks with a harder choice between containing inflation and supporting growth. Inflation can still erode purchasing power. Even if the overall inflation rate falls, the prices that matter most to an investor may rise faster than the headline measure. That makes it worth thinking about future spending needs, not just whether inflation is moving closer to a central bank’s target. Higher yields give investors more choices. High-quality bonds now offer more income than they did during the low-rate era, making them a more compelling option for investors seeking returns. Their prices can still fall if yields rise further, though, so a higher starting yield doesn’t remove short-term risk. Stocks and bonds may not always offset each other. When an inflation shock puts pressure on both asset classes, a traditional stock and bond portfolio may offer less protection than investors expect. Real assets and other diversifying strategies may be worth considering alongside that foundation, depending on an investor’s goals and risk tolerance. But the longer-term investment story is how countries respond, which often involves spending more on defense, energy security and supply chains they can depend on. Those efforts require substantial financing and may create opportunities for businesses that help make economies more resilient. Those opportunities are not confined to traditional defense companies – or to the United States. They span industries and regions, from chipmaking and manufacturing to power infrastructure and critical materials. But a more fragmented world also makes it more important to distinguish between countries that can finance their ambitions and companies that may benefit from the spending. "While geopolitical fragmentation can act as a drag on global growth, we also think it could lead to a meaningful increase in capital expenditure in both the public and private sectors, which can drive nominal growth," said Camporeale. "Investors must be selective about where countries sit on the spectrum of natural resources, vulnerabilities to supply bottlenecks, and their ability to defend themselves." Security spending could benefit companies across the globe. European businesses are capturing orders tied to rearmament and advanced technology. South Korea, Taiwan and Japan supply semiconductors and other equipment that countries need to expand their AI capabilities, while Mexico could benefit as companies move production closer to the United States. The opportunities differ by region, but all reflect a greater willingness to spend on security and reliable supply chains. A country’s vulnerabilities can change the investment case. Its ability to defend itself, develop AI infrastructure, obtain essential supplies and adapt to climate risks all matter. Europe shows why those distinctions are important: Companies could gain from spending on resilience, while the governments financing that spending may face pressure from higher debt and borrowing costs. Energy and critical materials remain potential bottlenecks. Building data centers, expanding power grids and strengthening domestic industries all require reliable energy and materials such as copper. Supply can take years to catch up with demand, making these resources important both to the AI buildout and to national resilience. Alongside their role in these industries, commodities may help diversify portfolios during periods when inflation weighs on both stocks and bonds. Gold offers a different way to navigate fragmentation. Some countries are seeking to hold more of their reserves outside the dollar-based system, and central banks are holding more gold as a share of their overall reserves. That shift could support demand for gold for reasons distinct from the need for energy and metals to build infrastructure. The first phase of the AI boom rewarded companies supplying the chips, equipment and power needed to execute it. Heading into 2027, the question is shifting from how much infrastructure can be built to whether enough people and businesses will use AI – and pay for it – to justify the investment. That doesn’t mean the AI opportunity is ending. AI could still boost productivity and corporate profits, but the scale of the buildout makes it more important to distinguish between companies that can turn demand into durable revenue and those counting on another surge in spending. "We assume that AI adoption may spur continued productivity gains as business use cases expand. AI needs to earn its keep by delivering real value to an economy rather than just answer questions," said Camporeale. "According to the firm’s 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, we believe the U.S. economy could see a 50% boost in productivity in the next 10-15 years. We believe hyperscalers may be well positioned to take advantage of this next phase of the AI trade from buildout to adoption." AI needs to move beyond early adopters. Businesses are experimenting with AI, but widespread use is still in its early stages. For the buildout to pay off, more companies will need to use AI in everyday work, and consumers will need to find uses they value. Adoption could slow if the technology falls short of expectations – or if job disruption and public opposition make its wider use harder to sustain. The buildout has a high revenue hurdle. J.P. Morgan Wealth Management estimates that, in the early 2030s, customers would need to spend roughly $2.9 trillion a year on AI to cover the costs of global data center capacity projected for the end of 2029. An illustrative estimate puts potential annual spending by businesses, consumers and governments at about $3.6 trillion. Neither figure is assured: Both depend on how much capacity is built, how widely AI is adopted and what customers ultimately pay. How companies finance AI matters. Large cloud providers generally have stronger balance sheets and more established businesses to help fund their investments. Some smaller companies rely much more heavily on borrowing to build capacity before they have the revenue to support it. If investors become less willing to finance those plans, access to capital could determine which projects move forward and which companies struggle. The next AI winners may look different from the first. Chipmakers and other infrastructure suppliers benefited as spending on the buildout repeatedly exceeded expectations. Further surprises may be harder to deliver as financing, power availability and resistance to new data centers constrain construction. But a slower build could also make scarce computing capacity more valuable. Major cloud providers may be well positioned because they both supply that capacity and sell services built on it; over time, companies that turn AI into products customers pay for could capture more value. The price of progress is becoming clearer. Building AI infrastructure and making economies more secure both require enormous amounts of capital, while inflation and higher interest rates have made that capital more expensive. For investors, the opportunity is not simply to fund those ambitions, but to be selective about which risks might be worth taking. That suggests considering a portfolio designed to pursue long-term growth without depending on every part of the AI buildout paying off or inflation fading smoothly. Not working with us yet?
